a2-present-er.title: Present Tense: -ER Verbs, Être, and Avoir
a2-present-er.pattern: je -e, tu -es, il/elle -e, nous -ons, vous -ez, ils/elles -ent
a2-present-er.explanation: Most French verbs end in -er (parler, manger, habiter) and follow one regular pattern: drop -er, add -e/-es/-e/-ons/-ez/-ent. "Être" (to be) and "avoir" (to have) are irregular and used constantly: je suis/j'ai, tu es/tu as, il est/il a, nous sommes/nous avons, vous êtes/vous avez, ils sont/ils ont.
a2-present-er.fact: "Avoir" is used in many expressions where English uses "to be": "avoir faim" (to be hungry, literally "to have hunger"), "avoir soif" (to be thirsty), "avoir raison" (to be right), "avoir vingt ans" (to be twenty years old).

dialogue.native: Tu parles très bien français !
dialogue.en: You speak French very well!

dialogue.native: Merci, j'habite ici depuis deux ans.
dialogue.en: Thanks, I've lived here for two years.

a2-ir-re-aller-faire.title: -IR/-RE Verbs, and Two Key Irregulars: Aller, Faire
a2-ir-re-aller-faire.explanation: Regular -ir verbs (finir, choisir) add -is/-is/-it/-issons/-issez/-issent. Regular -re verbs (vendre, attendre) add -s/-s/[nothing]/-ons/-ez/-ent. Two irregular verbs are essential from day one: "aller" (to go: vais/vas/va/allons/allez/vont) and "faire" (to do/make: fais/fais/fait/faisons/faites/font) — both used constantly in everyday speech and in set expressions.
a2-ir-re-aller-faire.fact: "Faire" appears in dozens of common expressions where English uses a completely different verb: "faire les courses" (to go grocery shopping), "faire du sport" (to play sports), "faire attention" (to pay attention), "faire beau/mauvais" (to be nice/bad weather).

dialogue.native: Qu'est-ce que tu fais ce week-end ?
dialogue.en: What are you doing this weekend?

dialogue.native: Je vais faire du sport et finir mes devoirs.
dialogue.en: I'm going to play sports and finish my homework.

a2-gender-agreement.title: Gender and Agreement: Nouns, Articles, and Adjectives
a2-gender-agreement.explanation: Every French noun is masculine or feminine, and articles and adjectives must agree: "le grand livre" (the big book, masc.), "la grande maison" (the big house, fem. — adjective gains an -e), "les grands livres"/"les grandes maisons" (plural, gains -s). Many adjectives change more irregularly in the feminine: "beau"→"belle", "nouveau"→"nouvelle", "blanc"→"blanche".
a2-gender-agreement.fact: Gender is mostly unpredictable and simply has to be memorized with each noun — but a few endings are strong hints: words ending in -tion, -sion, -té, -ette are almost always feminine ("la nation", "la beauté"), while words ending in -age, -ment, -eau are usually masculine ("le mariage", "le gouvernement").

dialogue.native: Cette nouvelle robe est vraiment belle.
dialogue.en: This new dress is really beautiful.

dialogue.native: Merci, et j'aime beaucoup ton nouveau manteau aussi.
dialogue.en: Thanks, and I really like your new coat too.

a2-reflexive.title: Reflexive Verbs: Actions Done to Oneself
a2-reflexive.explanation: Reflexive verbs describe an action the subject does to itself, and need a reflexive pronoun that matches the subject before the verb: "je me lève" (I get up, literally "I raise myself"), "tu te laves" (you wash yourself), "il se réveille" (he wakes up), "nous nous habillons" (we get dressed). Many everyday routine verbs in French are reflexive even when their English translation isn't.
a2-reflexive.fact: In the negative, "ne" goes before the reflexive pronoun and "pas" after the verb: "je ne me lève pas" (I don't get up) — the reflexive pronoun stays glued to the verb, not to "ne".

dialogue.native: Tu te lèves à quelle heure le matin ?
dialogue.en: What time do you get up in the morning?

dialogue.native: Je me réveille vers sept heures, puis je me douche.
dialogue.en: I wake up around seven, then I shower.

a2-passe-compose-avoir.title: Passé Composé: Talking About the Past with Avoir
a2-passe-compose-avoir.explanation: Most French verbs form their compound past tense with a present-tense form of "avoir" plus a past participle: "j'ai parlé" (I spoke/have spoken), "tu as fini" (you finished), "il a vendu" (he sold). Regular participles follow the verb ending: -er → -é, -ir → -i, -re → -u. This is the everyday past tense in spoken French — far more common than any literary past tense.
a2-passe-compose-avoir.fact: Many extremely common verbs have irregular participles that must be memorized: "avoir" → "eu", "être" → "été", "faire" → "fait", "voir" → "vu", "prendre" → "pris", "dire" → "dit", "écrire" → "écrit", "boire" → "bu".

dialogue.native: Qu'est-ce que tu as fait ce week-end ?
dialogue.en: What did you do this weekend?

dialogue.native: J'ai vu un film et j'ai lu un bon livre.
dialogue.en: I saw a movie and I read a good book.

a2-passe-compose-etre.title: Passé Composé with Être: Movement and Change Verbs
a2-passe-compose-etre.pattern: être (present) + past participle, agreeing in gender/number with the subject
a2-passe-compose-etre.explanation: About a dozen verbs — mostly involving movement or a change of state — use "être" instead of "avoir" in the passé composé, and their past participle must AGREE with the subject's gender and number: "il est allé" / "elle est allée" / "ils sont allés" / "elles sont allées". Common être-verbs: aller (go), venir (come), arriver (arrive), partir (leave), entrer (enter), sortir (exit), monter (go up), descendre (go down), naître (be born), mourir (die), rester (stay), tomber (fall).
a2-passe-compose-etre.fact: All reflexive verbs also use "être" in the passé composé, and generally agree the same way: "elle s'est levée" (she got up) — the -e is added because "elle" is feminine, even though "lever" itself doesn't take être when non-reflexive ("j'ai levé la main" — I raised my hand, uses avoir).

dialogue.native: Tu es arrivée à quelle heure hier soir ?
dialogue.en: What time did you arrive last night?

dialogue.native: Je suis rentrée vers minuit, un peu tard.
dialogue.en: I got home around midnight, a bit late.

a2-imparfait.title: Imparfait: Describing the Past — Habits and Background
a2-imparfait.explanation: The imperfect describes ongoing states, habits, and background scenery in the past — not a single completed event. Form it by taking the "nous" form of the present tense, dropping "-ons", and adding: -ais/-ais/-ait/-ions/-iez/-aient. "Nous parlons" → "je parlais" (I used to speak / I was speaking). "Être" is the only irregular stem: "j'étais", "tu étais", "il était"...
a2-imparfait.fact: The passé composé and imparfait are often used together in the same sentence, each doing a different job: the imparfait sets the scene ("il pleuvait" — it was raining) while the passé composé reports what happened in that scene ("quand je suis sorti" — when I went out): "Il pleuvait quand je suis sorti" (It was raining when I went out).

dialogue.native: Qu'est-ce que tu faisais quand j'ai appelé ?
dialogue.en: What were you doing when I called?

dialogue.native: Je regardais la télévision, il pleuvait dehors.
dialogue.en: I was watching television, it was raining outside.

a2-futur-proche.title: Futur Proche: The Near Future with Aller
a2-futur-proche.explanation: The easiest way to talk about the future in French is the "futur proche" (near future): a present-tense form of "aller" plus an infinitive: "je vais partir" (I'm going to leave), "elle va manger" (she's going to eat), "nous allons voyager" (we're going to travel). It works exactly like English "going to" and is far more common in everyday speech than the simple future tense.
a2-futur-proche.fact: In the negative, "ne...pas" wraps around the conjugated "aller", not the infinitive: "je ne vais pas partir" (I'm not going to leave) — the infinitive itself always stays untouched at the end.

dialogue.native: Qu'est-ce que vous allez faire ce soir ?
dialogue.en: What are you going to do tonight?

dialogue.native: On va dîner au restaurant, puis on va voir un film.
dialogue.en: We're going to have dinner at a restaurant, then we're going to see a movie.

a2-object-pronouns.title: Object Pronouns: Le/La/Les and Lui/Leur
a2-object-pronouns.pattern: direct: le/la/les (replace things/people) · indirect: lui/leur (replace "à + person")
a2-object-pronouns.explanation: Direct object pronouns replace a noun that directly receives the action, with no preposition: "le"/"la"/"les" (him/her/it/them) — "Je vois le livre" → "Je le vois". Indirect object pronouns replace "à + person": "lui" (to him/her) and "leur" (to them) — "Je parle à Marie" → "Je lui parle". Both types go directly BEFORE the conjugated verb, unlike English where the pronoun follows the verb.
a2-object-pronouns.fact: "Le", "la", and "les" also famously double as definite articles ("the") — context always makes clear which role they're playing, since articles precede nouns while pronouns precede verbs.

dialogue.native: Tu as vu mon frère récemment ?
dialogue.en: Have you seen my brother recently?

dialogue.native: Oui, je l'ai vu hier, et je lui ai parlé de toi.
dialogue.en: Yes, I saw him yesterday, and I talked to him about you.

a2-comparatives.title: Comparatives and Superlatives
a2-comparatives.pattern: plus/moins/aussi + adjective + que · le/la/les plus/moins + adjective
a2-comparatives.explanation: Comparisons use "plus...que" (more...than), "moins...que" (less...than), and "aussi...que" (as...as): "Elle est plus grande que moi" (She's taller than me), "Ce livre est moins cher que l'autre" (This book is cheaper than the other one). Superlatives add the definite article: "le plus grand" (the tallest), "la moins chère" (the least expensive).
a2-comparatives.fact: "Bon" (good) and "mauvais" (bad) have irregular comparative forms just like English "good/better/best": "bon" → "meilleur" (better) → "le meilleur" (the best), never "plus bon". "Mauvais" can go either way: "pire"/"le pire" (more common, more emphatic) or the regular "plus mauvais".

dialogue.native: Ce restaurant est meilleur que l'autre, non ?
dialogue.en: This restaurant is better than the other one, right?

dialogue.native: Oui, et c'est le meilleur du quartier, je pense.
dialogue.en: Yes, and I think it's the best in the neighborhood.
